topics.label: Introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and sets out what students should learn about cancer causation.

topics.label: Mutations, susceptibility and the evolution of cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations can give rise to evolving cancer clones depending on the susceptibility of the host cells and their environment.

topics.label: Environmental contributions to cancer risk
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the evidence that environmental exposures influence cancer risk rather than cancer being solely a matter of chance or inherited predisposition.

topics.label: Infectious causes of cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections contribute to carcinogenesis, with Burkitt lymphoma illustrating the interaction between pathogens and cancer-driving genetic changes.

topics.label: How environmental carcinogens damage DNA
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental exposures produce DNA damage and mutations, showing how their effects depend on activation and processing within the body.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish mutation-initiating activity from the promotion of tumour growth through a permissive cellular environment.

topics.label: Developmental and tissue specificity of carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how susceptibility to carcinogens depends on the biological context of exposure and consolidate the preceding account of context-dependent carcinogenesis.

topics.label: Evidence and methods for assessing carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how carcinogenic exposures can be identified and tested while assessing the limitations of the resulting evidence.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing draws together the lecture's conclusions about environmental cancer risks and the difficulty of assessing them to frame everyday risk–benefit decisions.
